sentences.text: The name Hainosaurus translates to 'lizard from the Haine', a reference to the river located near where the remains were first uncovered.
This creature is regarded as one of the largest mosasaurs, though scientific estimates of its total size have been adjusted several times over the years.
Its skeleton includes 53 vertebrae extending from the neck to the tail region where chevrons are found, a count significantly higher than the 35 vertebrae seen in the related genus Tylosaurus.
Consequently, the tail of Hainosaurus is shorter than that of Tylosaurus because it possesses fewer vertebrae that bear these chevron structures.
The estimated length of this animal has fluctuated dramatically, shifting from an original calculation of 17 meters down to a more recent figure of 12.2 meters.
The genus was originally described by Louis Dollo in 1885 following the discovery of a skeleton in a phosphate quarry near Mesvin, Belgium.
The specific epithet bernardi was chosen to honor Leopold Bernard, the industrialist who financed the excavation of the holotype skeleton — the specific specimen the species is based on.
This holotype skeleton is now preserved at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences under the catalog number IRSNB R23.
A second species, Hainosaurus pembinensis, was later described in 1988 by Elizabeth Nicholls based on fossils recovered in Manitoba, Canada.
To date, there are 16 recorded fossil occurrences of Hainosaurus listed in the Paleobiology Database.

While some documentaries suggest these animals traveled in large family groups, most experts believe Tylosaurinae and mosasaurs likely lived solitary lives, gathering only during mating or when mothers gave birth.
Hainosaurus is classified within the family Mosasauridae.
It belongs to the subfamily Tylosaurinae and is closely related to the genus Tylosaurus.
The authority for naming the genus is attributed to Dollo in 1885.
Fossils of Hainosaurus date from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
The animal lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, existing between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
In 2010, researchers Bullard and Caldwell argued that the specimen previously identified as Hainosaurus pembinensis actually belonged to the genus Tylosaurus due to a revised vertebral count.
Some scientists continue to debate whether Hainosaurus is a synonym of Tylosaurus, citing unexplored differences in tooth morphology, specifically an advanced cutting-based dentition.
